speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-158, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act (St. Luke 11:46).

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN MEMBER AND CITIZEN
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN MEMBER AND CITIZEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill proposes to remedy the grievance that arises when the public relationship between a member of parliament and a citizen is subverted to the private relationship between a lawyer and client to the financial hurt of the citizen; as when, for example, the citizen asks his member to make inquiries of the ministry in an immigration matter and is often dismayed to find that his member, being a lawyer, has billed him for fees on a solicitor-client basis.
This grievance is an ancient one and the remedy proposed is to revive and modernize an order of the United Kingdom that is 300 years old. I present this bill as a further contribution to the development of a code of ethics for members of the Senate and House of Commons, and trust it will receive the support of all parties in this house.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

1.	Why is the knowledge of the English language primarily required for the position of standards and methods officer, Civil Service Commission, competition number 66-0-523?

4.	Why does the Civil Service Commission not require bilingualism in all cases?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Secretary of State):
speechtext:
1, 2, 3. Competition 66-0-523 was the third competition advertised by the Civil Service Commission to recruit a methods and standards officer for the Department of Public Works, Ottawa. For each of the first two competitions, advertised in 1964 and 1965 respectively, a knowledge of both the English and French languages was required but neither competition attracted a qualified candidate willing to accept appointment. It was concluded that candidates with the desired technical and linguistic qualifications were not available. After carefully reviewing the needs of the department and the circumstances under which the duties would be performed, it was decided to require knowledge of English with knowledge of French considered an asset in the assessment of the candidates.
4.	The role of the commission as far as bilingualism is concerned is determined by section 47 of the Civil Service Act which does not require bilingualism in all cases.

The house resumed, from Thursday, March 24, consideration of the motion of Messrs. Byrne, Nugent, Scott (Danforth) and Stan-bury:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Criminal Code for the purpose of
(a)	abolishing the death penalty in respect of all offences under that act;
March 28, 1966

(b)	substituting a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment in those cases where the death penalty is now mandatory; and
(c)	providing that no person upon whom a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment is imposed shall be released from imprisonment without the prior approval of the governor in council.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset, as we resume consideration of the motion concerning the abolition of capital punishment, I want to say that it is an honour and privilege to take part in this debate. The question of capital punishment has been brought to the attention of the nation as never before, and as a result the eyes of Canadians across the nation are focussed on this debate.
It is no light matter for any one of us to be part of a decision which involves the lives of other human beings. Life moves forward constantly, and with it progress. The famous Danish critic, Kierkegaard said "Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards."
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Therefore we must seek to learn from the past in order that we may live safely and justly in the future. The spirit of the times is for change. Change is imperative if we would survive. The pattern of living things is for change. However, acknowledging that, I do not believe it means that we should reject those basic moral principles which have been the warp and woof of our heritage. I believe it is our duty to be progressive enough to understand the inevitability of change but conservative enough to accept the need for the continuity of basic principles particularly as they relate to fixed values and standards.
The question of capital punishment is one which arouses emotion in each of us. I am grateful for this non-partisan debate on the basis of personal conviction. I believe it has been of a very high standard and a credit to the house. Abolitionists and retentionists both claim evidence to support their arguments. Conflicting evidence confuses the picture. In my opinion the reason there is no convincing evidence on the subject is that it is difficult to measure man's mind. Therefore what we say is basically for the record as we explain the reason for our personal votes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but conversations are taking place in the chamber which make it very difficult to follow the hon. member.

Before proceeding further with the reasons for my own stand I must
,	Criminal Code
state that I cannot support the motion before us because I am convinced that it would be wrong to abolish the death penalty completely. It is interesting to note that while this motion would provide, if passed, for the abolition of the death penalty under the Criminal Code, it does not have this effect with regard to the death penalty as provided in other statutes. I am thinking specifically of the National Defence Act, sections 66,67,68,69, 70 and 71. It is a fact that section 66 of the National Defence Act makes the death penalty mandatory for certain offences against the state.
I cannot accept the statement repeated by several in this debate that to retain the death penalty is to cling to a hangover from the barbaric past. In my Christian faith I believe that human life is most sacred. Man was created in the image of God. In the commandments of Moses I am told by God not to kill. When others in my society accept this command with me, then I have personal safety of life as do my family and neighbours.
The sanctity of human life cannot be questioned. Christ has told us to love our neighbours. Murder, the taking of life, is not to be condoned. It is therefore the continuing responsibility of the Christian to interpret to those about us that every human being must have as his basic right not only justice before the law but also our personal understanding, respect and concern because he, like me, is a human being and our brother under one God, Creator of us all.
However, in determining my own stand on the question of abolition versus retention I cannot rely entirely on my own judgment. There are still those old-fashioned enough, and I am one of them, who believe that God has provided in His Word guidance to meet every problem which may confront us. In James 1:5 we read:
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
To me, at the root of every question the Scriptures must be our final authority, not my opinion or someone else's. It is not the reasoning of one who differs with me which must be my final guide. It is not the norm of what is considered the lowest common denominator of custom or current practice. It is not even what the church itself teaches, for again it is the Bible, not the church, which is the final authority. In my understanding of Scripture I find that capital punishment was

March 28, 1966
Criminal Code
intended by God as a penalty for those who take law and justice into their own hands or who for personal gain wilfully take the life of another person.
Prior to the days of Noah there was no death penalty. When Cain killed his brother Abel there was no such law and no such sentence was passed. He was banished from the Garden for life. Following this the descendants of Cain became part of a society which was grossly corrupt, rotten with sin and violence, and God sent death universally upon all but one family. Following the flood God says in Genesis 9:6:
Who so sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed; for in the image of God made he man.
Exodus 21:12 says the same thing:
He that smiteth a man, so that he die, shall be surely put to death.
Significantly this passage in many Bibles falls on the same page as the Ten Commandments which are the basis of our Canadian law and fundamental to the moral conduct of the individual. Some argue that the New Testament has changed this Old Testament teaching. They say the New Testament has replaced the "eye for an eye" philosophy with an ethic of love. However, the ethic of love theme of the New Testament applies only on a person to person basis, as do the Ten Commandments. The command to turn the other cheek cannot apply to law enforcement by the state; otherwise lawlessness would be encouraged. The right of the state to punish with death is more expressly established in chapter 13 of Romans, verses 1 to 5. Here the apostle Paul describes the law enforcement officials as "ministers of God" who "bear not the sword in vain".
Many Bible commentators, much more wise in their understanding of the Scriptures than myself, interpret this passage as supporting capital punishment. Among them are such men as Luther, Calvin, Hodge, Clarke, Moule, Meyer and Studd. Capital punishment is the traditional Christian position. It was also held by the Roman Catholic theologian, Thomas Aquinas. According to the Romans' passage, God gave the state the power of death for two reasons, first, to satisfy the demands of God's justice and, second, to serve as a protection to society by deterring crime in the future.
When the state takes the life of a capital offender it does so as God's agent, having received express authority from God. In the performance of law enforcement law officials 
are likewise responsible. Therefore it is as much a dereliction of duty for law officials to execute men who do not deserve death as it is to fail to execute criminals who deserve it. That does not mean that every capital offender must be executed. Far from it. The Bible permits and encourages justice to be tempered by mercy at times but not all the time.
Capital punishment is necessary for the good of society. I agree with Father W. J. Ring who said recently:
The whole function of government is to protect and to advance the common good, the welfare, of the civil community as a complete entity. This it does by legislation through the exercise of civil authority both in the making of laws for the common good and in seeing to it that the laws are kept by means of adequate and appropriate sanctions. Moreover, since man is by nature, and not simply by choice a civil animal, and his nature as such is from God, then God also is the source, in this sense, of the civil authority without which the common good and, consequently, the individual good of the citizen, cannot be achieved. Civil authority, then, is the exercise of divine authority in the civil sphere. It was for this reason, for example, that St. Paul could tell his people to be subject to their rulers.
Now since the government is charged with the duty of protecting and defending the common good it has, then, the right to use whatever legitimate means are required to preserve the common good which, after all, can only be the physical, emotional, moral and intellectual welfare of the civil community as a complete entity.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Consequently, it is obvious that the government has the right and the duty to defend the civil community from aggression from without, as in time of war, or from aggression from within, as from treason and the like. This is so, even though such a defence of the community may involve the taking of the life of the aggressor. Surely, if by way of the just defence of his own life a given citizen may take the life of one who is unjustly attacking him, a fortiori, the civil community, through the agency of government, may do the same thing when the life of the community is so endangered. A murderer is precisely that, an unjust aggressor with regard to the community, for in taking into his own hands the unlawful execution of another human being in this fashion he has thereby made an attack on the life of the community itself.
Dr. James M. Gray, the noted Bible scholar and Christian statesman of our parents' day, stated it well when he said:
The death penalty has been abused in almost all the countries of the world, but this does not justify its abolition in cases of premeditated homicide; and unwillingness to apply to the criminal the pain of death ordained by God himself, the author of life, always tends to the increase of crime and gives loose rein to personal vengeance. The inviolability of human life means that the life of a human being is a thing so sacred that he who takes it without just cause must pay for it with his own in amends to outraged justice, both human and divine. When, therefore, law makers abolish the death penalty for capital crimes, they
March 28, 1966

strike a blow at the very source and centre of real God-ordained government, and transgress an unrepealed law of God for the good of the race.
God placed upon man the great responsibility of self-government. This responsibility has never been taken away. The authority of the .state is subject to the sovereignty of God and it is man's duty to obey in all the instructions He has given and for this reason man has no authority to make his own choice against that of God. Clearly the commandment is that the state has the right to administer *capital punishment for premeditated, wilful murder, and I agree with the present *Criminal Code's differentiation between capital and non-capital murder, even as it is agreed that the state has the authority that it has to administer lesser punishment for lesser *crimes.
It is not correct to grant this responsibility as retribution or revenge. Retribution and state authority must be differentiated. The issue is between the administration of justice by the state and the individual. Punishment for a crime is the responsibility of the state; it is clearly the state's prerogative. There are those who have said in this debate that reformation and rehabilitation are the primary objectives of punishment. This therapeutic aspect is an important part but not all of it. Punishment also must have as its objective the cleansing and protection of society and the vindication of justice.
"Thou shalt not kill" is probably more correctly stated as "Thou shalt not murder." Murder is always killing, but killing is not always murder. Capital punishment is killing but it is not murder. It is, rather, the penalty for murder. Scripture defines murder: If a man hate his neighbour, and lie in wait for him, and rise up against him, and smite him mortally that he die-that is capital murder. In other words, murder is the direct result of unlawfully planning the death of another person, or where one person dies as a result of another person seeking to fulfil his own passions of greed or sex. It is worthy of note that the majority of today's murders fall into either of these two groupings. Perhaps the most common of the two is the gangster murder by the professional criminal.
The recent murder of lawyer Payette of Montreal is a good example, or the lime pit murders of the underworld in Quebec. Here the murderers make killing their business. They are men who weigh the benefits and the risks. They may even have their legal advisers. They, by specific intent, make a decision
Criminal Code
to eliminate certain people. Society, the common good, must be protected from such and capital punishment is the only effective penalty. Surely such criminals are not worthy of some therapeutic reform. I cannot but agree with former Royal Canadian Mounted Police Commissioner L. H. Nicholson, who said:
The criminal fraternity generally would welcome the abolition of capital punishment. I think the time has not yet come to abolish capital punishment.
The inquiry into the security of the nation promised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) may well be more important than any of the recent inquiries. Has international crime, the underworld of gangsterism, successfully penetrated the fibres of our society? Perhaps even the Munsinger inquiry has its importance in determining whether or not the real threat of the underworld posed itself in the person of a party call girl.
It is imperative that the channels of justice do everything in their power to make sure that men who are not guilty of murder do not die. As one regards the current book about the trial of Steven Truscott one wonders if in this case justice did do all it should have. The Bible warns about such cases.
The murderer shall be put to death by the mouth of witnesses: but one witness shall not testify against any person to cause him to die.
The moral law of God is perfect. Human beings are not perfect and do make mistakes. You and I do, we all do. However, I do not believe we should condemn what is sound law simply because of the imperfections and mistakes of human beings. Our society will be strengthened if we seek to uphold and honour the moral laws of God rather than repudiate and abolish them.
I respect the appeal the abolitionists have made in this debate. However, I believe their suggested solution is one which will have far greater and more serious consequences than those which the specific problem presents to us now. There are a few comments I should like to make regarding some of the arguments presented by those who support abolition.
First, it is said that capital punishment is not a deterrent. If capital punishment appears to be not much of a deterrent the reason is that a lot of the sting has been taken out of it. Although crime has steadily increased the use of the death penalty has steadily decreased. Practice in Canada during recent years is equivalent to the abolition of

March 28, 1966
Criminal Code
capital punishment. It is for this reason that I believe the resolution before us must be permitted to come to a vote. I had intended at first to move an amendment but as the debate has progressed I have become convinced that the question has been well put. This debate, therefore, should be terminated without undue extension by a specific vote.
It is argued also that society should be concerned about the redemption of the criminal, a redemption that might be prevented by an execution. However, by the same argument society should be concerned for the safety and welfare of potential murder and rape victims. One of Caryl Chessman's targets, a 17 year old girl, was subjected to brutal depravity for four hours. Twelve years later she was still in a trance with little hope of recovery. Jack Graham blew up an airliner containing his mother and 43 innocent victims. How much opportunity did these victims have to prepare for eternity, for eternal redemption?
On the other hand, there needs to be more concern for crime prevention. Is it reasonable to campaign strongly for the possibility of the redemption of murderers, most of whom have a long record of violent crime, while millions of pliable minds watch men and women being stabbed, shot, strangled, drowned, poisoned, and maltreated in almost every possible way as often as 20 times a day on television? If those who lead the movements for abolition are really concerned for the sacredness of life they should do something about the disrespect shown for life on television programs and in movies, which do so much to influence pliable minds.
It appears that with a decrease in the severity of punishment for criminals comes a corresponding increase in crime and the suffering of the innocent. In recent years, for example, the number of policemen murdered by felons has been larger than the number of felons executed by the state. It is argued that the administration of capital punishment is attended by many abuses. This may be so. The same can be said of the administration of Christian churches. Do we, therefore, eliminate the Christian churches? No, we try to eliminate the abuse. The same appproach applies to the abuses of capital punishment.
Abolitionists make much of the loss of innocent lives through the death penalty. They overlook the fact, however, that more innocent lives have been lost through non-executed criminals who remained alive to commit more crimes than through executed non-criminals.

It has been said that the science of penology as well as the improvements in standards of social work and law enforcement have advanced to the point where society is protected to a greater extent than by the imposition of capital punishment. It is true that we have more effective police forces and more thorough rehabilitation of criminals. However, of the 14 states in the United States which abolished capital punishment prior to 1962, 8 have reinstituted it. Penology does give more protection now than formerly against criminals committing crimes in the future, but it cannot protect against persons committing crime in the first instance.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Every one of us, Mr. Speaker, still reflects the image of God. To murder a man is still an outrage, an outrage against God, the Creator, against man, the victim, against the victim's loved ones, against society and against the institution of government. Because life is sacred, Mr. Speaker, life must be protected against maltreatment and murder. Policemen charged with the enforcing of the laws of the state must have the right to kill in self-defence or in the interest of law enforcement. The state must punish severely, at times with death, those who wilfully disregard the sacredness of the lives of others.
I believe this is necessary for the general good of society.

Mr. Speaker, let me say at once that I would join only to a very limited extent with what has been said by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), but I do agree with him with regard to the quality of this debate. In answer to those who have made accusations in respect of standard of debate in this house I say that the strength of argument, exercised with restraint, and the eloquence which has gone hand in hand with common sense have been a great tribute to the members who have participated during the two days through which this debate has progressed. The subject is a tremendously difficult one. I hasten at once to say that I completely disagree with the hon. member for Red Deer as to his conclusion, the way in which he has arrived at his conclusion and as to the way he is going to vote.
One can not dismiss from one's mind, Mr. Speaker, all of the wisdom which lies within the four corners of the Scriptures, but in respect of the religious considerations in regard to this matter God has endowed me with some intelligence and set me upon a path
March 28, 1986

along which I have derived some experience. In coming to a decision in an issue of this kind I would be derelict in my duty if I failed to take into consideration the knowledge and experience I have derived during the course of my life and my career. Having done this, I can come to no other conclusion, Mr. Speaker, than that I must support this resolution.
I have taken a little time to look through the debates of Wednesday and Thursday of last week and I think a rather remarkable phenomenon appears from a reading of what has been said. I am particularly interested in what has been said by those who have taken the opposite view to mine and who, generally, seem to favour retention. The phenomenon is this, Mr. Speaker. If you examine carefully what most of these members have said-this applies particularly to those who appear at first blush to have been very strong proponents of a measure of retention-you will find somewhere in their speeches indications of doubt, of qualification, of conditional acceptance. In my opinion, if there is to be an onus in an issue of this kind the onus should be upon those who urge that capital punishment be retained. I think the act of taking life is so unnatural, so abnormal and so repugnant that those who argue even for the right of the state to take life must be prepared to discharge that onus.
Here, Mr. Speaker, we find in this chamber those who argue for the retention of capital punishment qualifying their statements. I have a few of the comments before me but I am not going to relate them to the hon. members who made them. One hon. member said: "The supreme penalty should be enacted only after guilt is established beyond a shadow of a doubt and only for wanton, wilful and premeditated murder".
As you know, Mr. Speaker, and as other hon. members know, today guilt must be established in any criminal offence beyond a reasonable doubt. If capital punishment were to be inflicted only upon those who were convicted within the four corners of this qualification, I think capital punishment would never be carried out. The hon. member said that guilt must be established "beyond a shadow of a doubt". This shadow of a doubt must be applied to each specific area of the charge. It must be established beyond a shadow of a doubt that it was wanton murder, that it was wilful murder and that it was premeditated murder. The hon. member who made that statement may not know it but I
Criminal Code
suggest he has a strong doubt in his own mind as to the necessity of preserving capital punishment.
Another hon. member said: "So long as human sciences are what they are I think it might be wise to wait". Then there is the qualification: "Let us not do it now; let us wait a little while. Let us have another parliament abolish capital punishment." Another hon. member said: "I have reached the conclusion that now is not the time to abolish capital punishment". Another hon. member said: "I think it must be retained because we are not ready for abolition". And so it goes.
I would direct my remarks, Mr. Speaker, to those hon. members who are still wrestling with their consciences, those hon. members who are gripped in the agony of irresolution in an attempt to come to a proper decision in this matter. I suggest that if those who are urging that capital punishment must be retained can do so only in qualified terms of this kind, then they have failed to establish a case by that standard which we in this chamber should expect in an issue of this sort.
Let it be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that in this debate we are holding in our hands the highest of all human responsibilities, that of life and death. It is for us to lay down the rules which can spin out the golden thread of life or snap it off each time a trapdoor opens to hurl a living, breathing human being into the darkness of eternity. I know there are those who say and are quite entitled to say that we will do this only to those who in turn have taken life.
But this distinction must be made. Ours will not be the tortured, twisted and unnatural action, sometimes only an emotional muscular reflex, which comes from the gloomy recesses of the mind of man who has killed. Ours is, or should be, the calm, reasoned, cold and calculated volition, the collective act of those who are the repository of the wisdom of all the people in the state. For us there can be no refinements, no subtleties, no distinctions, no recommendation for mercy, no excuse. Let this be understood.
I suggest that there can be no clearer way of bringing this home to the attention of the house than to put it this way. If we fail to pass this measure substantially in its present form, then whether we like it or not we are directly and intimately concerned with all the consequences. It is of no avail to say that the law is there and that it ought to be a matter

March 28. 1966

of applying it, of letting the law taking its course. We are the law. We make the law; we change the law or we leave the law relating to capital punishment as it is. I suggest that if we retain capital punishment we must be prepared in our minds to spend the last hours with those who are condemned and awaiting execution, to walk with them to the scaffold, to watch the hangman securing the noose, and to wait for the end. We are a part of this and we cannot rationalize or raise specious arguments to avoid this consequence.
I say this, Mr. Speaker, as solemnly as I can. The decision in an issue of this kind, made by the yeas and the nays which will be cast when we vote on this resolution, cannot be supported on anything but our own consciences. We should listen to our constituents, read the writings of others and review the debate not only on this particular resolution but on others which have gone before. This is right and this we can and must do. But the ultimate decision must be made by each one of us in the loneliness of his own conscience.

Mention has been made of the fact that there has been a possibility of error creeping into criminal trials and this has been linked to the Truscott case. Generally speaking, I have confidence in our courts, in our judges and in our system of justice, and my view in this regard is derived from almost 40 years of practising law mainly in the criminal courts of this land. But, Mr. Speaker, this is only relative praise. Our system is not perfect. In my opinion it is only the least imperfect system of any systems of justice that I know. There is room for error. There have been miscarriages of justice. Innocent men have been sent to jail. Men have been hanged when the sentence imposed on them should have been reduced. Also, I believe innocent men have been executed.
However, I would rather discuss the extension of this principle to something distinct from though related to the simple black or white of guilty or not guilty. Let there be a certain set of facts which could be, and I emphasize the words "could be", proved. Does this mean that under any possible conditions the same result, the same verdict, the same sentence would always be brought about? By no means. There are wide possibilities for variation.
The choice of the charge to be laid is a choice which lies within the range of an individual or within the range of several

individuals. For example, in my own province of Alberta it is the Attorney General who decides on the basis of a certain set of facts which have been brought out in a preliminary hearing whether the charge will be manslaughter, non-capital murder or capital murder. Also of importance are the character of the judge, the make-up of the jury, the character, ability, experience and background of counsel for the defence and to a lesser extent of crown counsel.
I say on my full responsibility and with all the solemnity I can command, basing my opinion in large measure on my own personal knowledge, that out of the same set of facts it is likely and in fact possible that different combinations of these external collateral conditions can bring about a verdict of not guilty, a verdict of guilty of manslaughter, a verdict of guilty of non-capital murder, a verdict of guilty of capital murder with a recommendation for mercy or a verdict of guilty of capital murder with execution to follow. I have always had an uneasy feeling, despite the strides we have made in our system of jurisdprudence and in spite of the progress we have made in the administration of justice, that in our trials and in our administration of justice there still remains much of the quality of a gamble. There still remains something of the nature of a game of roulette. We can never be certain that the ball is going to drop into the proper slot.
One is tempted to draw on one's personal experience to support this view. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I can do no better than to refer to an incident in a most fascinating book called "For the Defence", which is a biography of the great English advocate, Sir Edward Marshall Hall, superbly put together by another lawyer, Edward Marjoribanks. In the book it is set out how in one of his earlier cases Marshall Hall defended a young working girl who had been seduced by a married man. She bore an illegitimate child. Soon after the birth of the child she told the nurse not to mind the baby but to attend to her, the mother. Ten days later the young mother was sitting with the nurse and her baby and said, "How can anyone get rid of a baby like that?" Shortly afterward the mother took the baby up to bed and the child was never again seen alive.
The police traced the mother and an inspector took a statement from her in which she said, "I will tell you the truth. I killed it. I did not know what to do with it. I put it in a box. You will find it up there." The mother
March 28, 1966

was charged with wilful murder and admitted the charge. The law being what it was, she was indicted for murder. Her counsel called no evidence and his entire defence was elicited through cross-examination.
The mother's remark at the confinement was accounted for by the fact that she had not seen the child and her maternal instincts had not been aroused. Her remark about getting rid of the baby was shown in a completely new light when the two nurses called by the prosecution admitted that the emphasis fell upon the word "Can" and that the actual words were "How can anyone get rid of a little baby like this?" This, together with the admission that the mother was kissing and feeding her child, completely contradicted the interpretation suggested by the prosecution.
As to the other statement attributed to the mother, the whole meaning of it is changed by making the middle sentence refer to the last part and not to the first. In other words, having killed the child accidentally by overlaying it in bed she admitted this and then said she did not know what to do with it and had put it in a box. As to the admission of wilful murder, the inspector admitted that he had made a mistake and had never charged her with wilful murder, but merely with causing the death of the child.
In that case a brilliant defence counsel with a sense of timing and drama who had recently suffered a similar tragedy in his own life, conducted the defence. Presiding at the trial was an outstanding and sympathetic judge and a sympathetic jury. The verdict was the right one. However, I do suggest it is quite possible, and in another case it might have happened, that had counsel for the defence attempted to exclude the statements he would have been unsuccessful and the result would have been, as happens in eight cases out of ten, a verdict of murder.
This, of course, is a case where justice was done. However, I can recall a case in which I participated some years ago, Mr. Speaker, where a young boy of 19 was tried, convicted and ultimately executed. This happened well over 30 years ago. In that particular case the evidence was strongly consistent, in my opinion, with insanity and certainly with a verdict of manslaughter. The jury brought in a verdict of guilty of murder with a strong recommendation for mercy. The boy was ultimately executed.
Many years later I had the opportunity to discuss this case with one of the jurors who
Criminal Code
had come to see me. He told me that the trial jury had been dominated by one strong-minded individual who had an almost pathological aversion to any crime which included robbery and violence. It happened that in this case robbery with violence was not the motive. At least, it was not the primary motive. It happened that after the crime the boy had put on a pair of pants and a shirt belonging to the deceased. In the pants was 50 cents. It was in this sense that this man on the jury took it that there had been robbery with violence and he dominated the proceedings to such an extent that the verdict of guilty of murder was brought in. The rest of jurors salved their consciences by bringing in a recommendation for mercy which was not acted on. The boy was hanged.
This sort of thing does happen in our murder trials. In our system of penology and parole there is always some hope for righting a wrong and for making the punishment fit the crime, if necessary after the event. But we cannot awake the dead to say that we are sorry, that we must have made a mistake and that we really did not mean to hang you. I suggest that on vagaries such as this, on such slender reeds as this, rests the issue of life and death. Can we safely entrust to these arrangements the lives of any members of our society? True, they are imperfect members but imperfect members of an imperfect society for which we must at least accept our share of collective responsibility.
All of us have, with concern and with anxiety, studied the history of this grizzly subject of capital punishment and I conclude on this note, Mr. Speaker. We must conclude that there has been a slow but inexorable move toward the lessening of the use of this barbaric and outmoded instrument of execution which, despite arguments to the contrary, is still in the minds of too many people the weapon of retribution and vengeance. Can anyone really doubt that the end result of these proceedings will be, as in other civilized states, the abolition of the death penalty? Why then should Canada be among the last to act in its abolition? Mr. Speaker, let us do it now.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to take part in the debate, not, as must be obvious to all hon. members, as a member of the cabinet but as a member of the House of Commons speaking on a private member's

Throughout my remarks, which I anticipate will be brief, I will try not to reflect in any way upon matters which I have learned as a Privy Councillor and member of the government though it will be appreciated that it is difficult to set aside such experience.
If one must characterize one's position in this debate, my views are somewhere between those of the last two speakers. If you look at the subject from the point of view of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) I am a retentionist; if you look at it from the point of view of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) I am an abolitionist.
Murder is foul whenever it occurs. In the scale of our crimes it is and has always been the highest, the most hideous and the most hated by our people. Throughout the history of Canada and even before, by reason of the form of law we have followed many punishments have been exacted upon those who have taken the lives of others, some of them so horrible that nowadays we can hardly believe that sentient men and women would resort to drawing and quartering, rending limb from limb and similar penalties. We have a scale of punishment for every offence under the law. Our laws are framed for the preservation of the balance of our society and, of course, to protect our social structure. We attach different penalties to different offences, ranging from a kind of supervision, something we call a suspension of a sentence, through monetary fines and periods of incarceration to the death penalty which we now retain as the final punishment for the taking of a life.
The temptation is easy to take a Biblical approach and to characterize any retentionist as a person who requires only that "vengeance be mine". Yet I think the word "vengeance" probably does not apply to anyone in our society with the possible exception of a person who feels himself or herself individually aggrieved, a person who is likely to be a close relative of a murder victim. We feel gradations of revulsion with regard to crimes. We feel gradations of revulsion even about civil matters involving offences against society. It seems to me-and I say this for the peace of my conscience-that there are some crimes, some kinds of murder which cry out for the ultimate penalty. Again, this is not a matter of wreaking vengeance but an expression of a punishment which is the top of the scale, the only way in which in our society

we can move to keep our social structure as we would have it. This means there are cases of willful killing for which I would not require the death penalty to be meted out. When I spoke in this chamber in 1961 while the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) was minister of justice it may be recalled that when killings were being divided into capital and non-capital murder it was a suggestion of mine that the murder of a prison official should be regarded as a type of capital murder.
It seems to me that if we are to retain our social structure positive measures must be taken to protect men such as police officers who risk their lives for our protection. Measures must be taken to protect our prison guards, those ill-paid individuals who need to be constantly on the qui vive to protect society from the occupants of prison cells. Then there must be some means of protecting society against those who commit murder for the second time. I believe this latter category is rare. I believe experience has shown that only in very few instances do people acquire a taste for killing and then kill again. But records show that such cases exist.
In these three categories it seems to me society needs the death penalty, bearing always in mind that I speak of those who are sane, of those who have not successfully raised the defence of insanity. Speaking from my own conscience, I believe the death penalty should be imposed for these classes of murder.
What I say in this regard is nothing new. Many hon. members have singled out the same classes of people. But, since I believe there must be a gradation of penalty to correspond with a gradation of crime, my conscience compels me to speak about a special kind of murder, revulsion to which may arise, I will readily admit, as much from the fact of my own sex as from my experience of 16 years at the bar. In addressing myself to this resolution I feel I would have to vote against it and of course against any amendment save an amendment that would retain within the law those classes of cases which I have had an opportunity to cite. Mr. Speaker, since last Wednesday several hon. members have expressed their views on the death penalty and the following resolution: Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Criminal Code for the purposes of (a) abolishing the death penalty in respect of all offences under that act;
(b)	substituting a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment in those cases where the death penalty is now mandatory; and
(c)	providing that no person upon whom a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment is imposed shall be released from imprisonment without the prior approval of the governor in council.
The present resolution contains three propositions. I am against paragraphs (a) and (b) because, in my humble opinion, the death penalty must be maintained a while longer.
I would be in favour of paragraph (c) because it would be appropriate for the governor in council, rather than the parole board, to decide about changing a sentence of life imprisonment or perpetual imprisonment in cases where such action has been considered until now.
But, since the movers of the resolution did not present it in such a way as to allow

Criminal Code
separate votes and you, Mr. Speaker, following a point of order I raised last Wednesday, supported by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), decided not to separate the resolution as far as the votes were concerned, I will vote against the said resolution.
We are given the occasion to ask for the retention of the death penalty or its abolition. I will be brief for two main reasons: first of all, my position on that subject has been well known in the house since 1958 and there is no conclusive reason for me to change it today. Moreover, we must not prolong the debate in order to allow the government to introduce as soon as possible very urgent measures to fight poverty, namely by increasing old age pensions, family allowances and reducing taxes in favour of Canadians with a low income as well as fighting inflation and increases in the cost of living. I hope that in his budget speech tomorrow night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) will meet the wishes of millions of citizens.
Mr. Speaker, on May 30, 1958, I made a speech in the House of Commons in favour of the retention of capital punishment. At that time, I stressed the provisions of our Criminal Code which seem marked with secular wisdom, with many judicial precautions and consecutive legal appeals. I showed also that capital punishment was an effective deterrent against murder, an appropriate retribution, a protection for the administration staff of our prisons and a means to avoid the proliferation of professional criminals. In conclusion, I said then that capital punishment must not be abolished as long as our customs and institutions would not make it necessary, and as long as the great majority of our Canadian people did not require such a change.
In 1961, our parliament gave a clear definition of capital murders, that is murders with premeditation, and non-capital murders. Today, I can see no definite argument which would convince me to change my stand.
However, I want to make it clear that, in my mind, capital punishment is not so much a necessary punishment than a means to set an example and to effectively prevent capital murder, treason and piracy.

Some members used statistics from foreign countries to support their argument, to illustrate the decrease or increase in the number of murders as a result of abolition or retention of capital punishment.

We must not judge solely by such data, for figures do not give the same results throughout the world, and it must be recognized that various countries reflect historical, political, social and psychological differences.
Let us, however, recall that England abolished capital punishment in 1964 and that, since then, murders have increased by one third, to such an extent, in fact, that on January 29 last, hundreds of thousands of Englishmen launched an active campaign in favour of reinstating it.
Here, in Canada, and more specifically in Quebec, according to the provincial Minister of Justice, Claude Wagner, who said so at Verdun, at a banquet held on January 30 last, there are twice as many murders since Ottawa has multiplied commutations of death penalty. The same is probably true for the other provinces.
It is advisable, under the circumstances, to retain capital punishment and to demand that the governor general in council, that is the federal cabinet, assume its responsibilities and apply the present law in its entirety. If the members of the federal cabinet commute death penalties because, in their innermost heart they want abolition, then let them speak out now and vote according to their conscience. But I would ask them to quit playing hide-and-seek and systematically making the present laws inoperative.
Capital punishment remains the best answer to capital and sordid murders, as the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) so ably pointed out a while ago, the first deterrent for thousands of citizens against such crimes. This is so true that people who deal with law courts, in whom armed bandits confide, know full well that a large number of bandits do not load their revolvers before committing a robbery, for fear that, in the excitement of the criminal operation, they might kill someone and hang for it later on.
It remains that some hardened murderers who have not been rehabilitated due to lack of advanced psychiatric knowledge, are known to be a permanent menace to society. It should be remembered that prison guards and other inmates are also members of society. If a life sentence is the only punishment for such murderers, in many cases they will try to escape. To achieve this, they will not hesitate at all to kill a guard or an over talkative partner. If justice nabs them again for naught save life, all they have to say is: "Put it on the bill. What's a murder more or less. Let society keep on feeding me in spite
March 28. 1966

of my crimes and escapes and the permanent menace that I am."
I have no objections to certain judicial reforms to enable every citizen, accused or sentenced for life under the provisions now in force, if they lack sufficient money for an adequate defence, to benefit from the same legal advantages now enjoyed by the Crown. In every case where mandatory death sentence is involved, the state should cover all legal costs of a full defence and, in addition, give the accused or the condemned without means the choice of counsel.
Furthermore, I would look with favour on the suggestion that the criminal now standing condemned for life come under the governor in council as far as his liberation is concerned. In such serious and far reaching cases, the responsibility of a decision should rest with those directly responsible to the people as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin), the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) and the members of the Federal Cabinet and not with the untouchable commissioners of the Parole Board.
Certain acts could also be improved and adapted to the developments of modern science. I am referring specifically to the evidence required on mental cases. Finally, rehabilitation methods could be improved.
But whatever reforms are suggested, capital punishment must be maintained in the statutes and fully implemented. I beg to differ from the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Pelletier) who maintained, on Thursday last, that we have now achieved a sufficient degree of civilization and progress to solve capital murders and murders for gain by means other than capital punishment.
I am deeply convinced that man, by his nature, will always be a human being and not a god, a being torn within himself between good and evil, and that his degree of civilization or moral refinement will always be in doubt.
As representatives of the people, we must take public opinion into account. That is why at the end of last January, through the newspapers of my county, I sounded the electorate of the county of Sherbrooke, with the following result:
Of 541 answers received, 475 or 88 per cent were in favour of retaining capital punishment; 66 answers or 12 per cent wanted capital punishment abolished.

50 per cent favoured hanging; 18 per cent, the electric chair; 11 per cent, the gas chamber; 13 per cent, the injection; .4 per cent, the guillotine; 2.6 per cent, shooting; 1 per cent, other methods and 1 per cent left it to the choice of the condemned man.
The Junior Chamber of Commerce of Sherbrooke also questioned its 210 members on this subject at the beginning of last February and 73 per cent of the answers were in favour of retaining capital punishment.
Therefore, for the reasons given in my speech in this house on May 30, 1958 and in view of the additional explanations which I gave today, I shall vote against the present resolution I want capital punishment to be retained as long as psychiatry and psychology do not succeed in making sane and well-adapted individuals out of those who commit premeditated and horrible murders.

Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons, for the three days during which this debate has been taking place, has been discussing a matter of very great and urgent concern not only to those here but to the country as a whole. In a debate of this kind, as indeed in any debate, it is only to be expected that members will take different positions for different reasons. We will, therefore, be in disagreement. I am in disagreement with many of those who have spoken or with the position they have taken or have indicated they will take. But we all proceed on the assumption that in this debate at any rate our disagreements and differences of opinion do not involve any questioning of motives and that we respect the motives and positions taken by others. The sincerity of the motives of everyone who has participated in the debate is demonstrated by the quality of the speeches which have been made.
Notwithstanding that feature of this debate and notwithstanding the importance of the subject we are dealing with and the decision that has to be made, I have a growing feeling that the House of Commons should not be asked to vote on this matter after only three days of debate which, as now has been indicated, is all the time that will be made available. Speaking for myself, I have to say with respect to the motion that if it comes to a vote I have not yet heard sufficient evidence to convince me that the law should be changed as the motion would change it.
Hear, hear.

If I have to vote on the motion I will therefore vote against it. I shall, as I know every other member will, vote with a clear conscience. I think I can fairly say that I am not in the habit of avoiding issues or ducking or evading responsibilities. If I have to vote I shall, and I will do so with a clear conscience but with a very great feeling of concern because I do not think we should be voting on the motion at this time. I know that the concern I feel, which makes me take this position and which leads to make my suggestion, is not a unique concern. I know it is felt by all members, although perhaps in the greatest measure by those who, like me, will feel compelled to vote against the motion if it comes to a vote.

Great concern would be felt by me if we had to vote because I do not think the evidence has been sufficient to cause me to approve of the motion. I do not think the arguments that have been advanced enable us to make up our minds. Particularly I think it is not a sound argument and yet it has been advanced-this is what bothers me-to say that the retention of capital punishment would be evidence of a continuation in Canada of some sort of barbaric society. I think this is not the kind of argument that should be used in this kind of debate, at least not in an attempt to convince others to change their minds, because if we vote to retain the death penalty it is not because we like to have it. Who is to suggest that anyone who votes that way takes any pleasure in the contemplation of the execution even of the most brutal murderer? We would vote that way because we believe that the retention of capital punishment, at this stage at any rate, is necessary for the protection of society and that no other means sufficiently adequate have yet been established.
In this connection, in support of my position I do not rest my case on the argument of the deterrent effect of capital punishment. I

rest it rather on the ground of protection from those who have shown a readiness to commit or procure the commission of a deliberate and planned killing. It is in this respect that I speak of the protection of society. I should like, therefore, to discuss the matter for a few minutes in the context of that approach and in the context of the law as it now stands as a result of the changes made in 1961.
In the course of the debate on the amendment to the Criminal Code which I had the honour of introducing when I was minister of justice in 1961, I attempted to elaborate and state as a philosophy, if you like, the concept upon which in my mind that amendment was based. I refer to the amendment which divided killings into two types, non-capital murder and capital murder.
I am not going to rehearse all those arguments at this time, although I have re-read them, but I have seen no compelling evidence to lead me to believe that the argument is not sound and does not form a sound basis for the retention of capital punishment. I am not suggesting that the law as it was amended in 1961 and as it now stands is perfect. By no means do I suggest that. Law is always susceptible to change and improvement. But surely we are entitled to be convinced by argument that the change suggested is an improvement before we simply adopt it for the purpose of change in itself.
It is therefore, I think, only right that we should remind ourselves what the law of 1961 did and how it now stands. One thing it did was to eliminate from liability to the death penalty many of the types of murders which some hon. members seem to have used as the basis of their arguments for the abolition of capital punishment. The change in the law in 1961 eliminated from suffering the death penalty a person who had committed murder and might be described as psychotic. It provided that capital murder was the only type of murder to which the death penalty was applicable.
In other words, by that change it is provided that unless the crime which results in a killing or the killing itself is planned and deliberate, the murder is non-capital. If the killing is carried out by an insane person there is, of course, still the absolute defence of insanity. If it is carried out by a person in a sudden fit of passion there is, quite apart from the defence of provocation, the necessity for the Crown now to prove that it was done in a planned and deliberate fashion, and if it
March 28, 19SG

can be established that it was done in a fit of sudden passion that element is not proven. In other words, Mr. Speaker, if the crime is totally unpremeditated, then it is not capital murder. That important change was made, and it seems to me to have been overlooked by many of those who have spoken in support of this motion.
Further, even if the murder is capital and the jury finds that the accused was guilty of a planned and deliberate killing, there is the important change made as a result of the law of 1961 that the jury must be asked whether they have any recommendation to make as to leniency or mercy. The jury must be asked that question. The purpose of inserting this provision was precisely to take care of the case in regard to which the jury had any doubt so that even if they felt it was capital murder within the definition, if there was something about it, some surrounding factor which would cause them to recommend leniency, they could do so. Even although they had found the accused was not insane within the legal definition of insanity, yet they might not be sure that his mental state was such that he should in fact suffer capital punishment as a consequence of his crime.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to observe that I am not happy about the definition of insanity as still carried forward in our Criminal Code. I refer to the old M'Naghten rule. I think this is one area which should be studied and possibly changed. This is another reason why I think this motion is inadequate and does not enable us really to get at the roots of the problem with which we should be dealing if we are to deal conclusively with the matter of capital punishment. I observed recently reports in American periodicals of a recommendation made as a result of an extensive study of the definition of insanity by the American Bar. I am very much influenced by that recommendation, which seems to me to be a great forward step in the legal treatment of insanity.
Coming back to the question of our law as it now stands, another important change made in 1961, which seems to me to go a good distance to meeting many of the arguments that have been advanced by those who have spoken in favour of the resolution, was that we provided for an automatic appeal court review. It does not matter whether the accused is rich or poor. If convicted of capital murder he not only has the right but the appeal court has the duty to review the case and the transcript of the evidence not only
Criminal Code
with respect to matters of law but the adequacy of the procedure and the facts as well. This is so whether or not the accused makes application for appeal. In addition to the reveiw by the court of appeal which is carried out automatically the accused has the right as a right-he does not need leave-to go to the Supreme Court of Canada, the highest court in the land. His case can be heard there whether he is rich or poor. He does not have to apply for leave.
Another very important change that was made and which I think should be borne in mind when we consider our position with respect to the motion was that in 1961 we inserted a provision in the law that no one under the age of 18 years could suffer pain of death by hanging. Even though convicted of capital murder such a person cannot be sentenced to be hanged. So, Mr. Speaker, while I make no further observation on the Truscott case at this point I simply say that Steven Truscott could not have been sentenced to hang after the 1961 change in the law.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
These, sir, are some of the factors I think should be borne in mind when we ask ourselves whether we are yet convinced that the law with respect to capital punishment as it now stands should be changed. I have said that in my view the philosophical arguments in support of the retention of capital punishment rest on the basis of the protection of society from those who would deliberately challenge society's supreme ordinance, the only basis on which a well ordered society can rest, namely, that no individual has the right to take a life. I say that society must be protected against those who would deliberately challenge that law. I am satisfied that this is quite a different argument from the argument which says that capital punishment should be retained because it deters would-be murderers from killing. Obviously it does not because people still kill. You cannot say it is a completely effective deterrent. Nor in my view, however, can you say it has not deterrent effect. Unfortunately you cannot prove the case one way or the other statistically, as it were. It is for this reason I say that it never seemed to me to be a sound basis upon which to rest a firm position. I think the basis of the protection of society against those who have defied society's supreme law is a sound philosophical basis.

March 28. 1966
Criminal Code
Other arguments were advanced which in my view leave room for the kind of uncertainties about which I have spoken and the kind of uncertainties which I would feel if I were compelled to vote now. These arguments are based on the statistics relating to the number of murders and the disposition of capital cases after there has been a conviction. I think it is important in the light of what we are discussing to examine some of these statistics. I shall only look at those since 1961 when the change was made to distinguish between capital and non-capital murder.
I should like, first, to look at the statistics with regard to the commutation or disposition of these cases because I think the statistics here indicate there is another area or another kind of uncertainty about whether some change should be made in the present law. I am alluding to the same facts as were referred to by the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), namely, that perhaps there should be greater certainty introduced into the circumstances under which the prerogative of mercy may be exercised.
I have referred to the change that had the result that a person convicted of capital murder is now convicted only of deliberate killing and we still have the additional safeguard of asking the jury whether or not they have any recommendation to make. It was certainly my thought, and I speak here only as an individual and do not say the law carries this interpretation, that when there came before any government of which I might be a member or others might be members a case where there was a conviction for capital murder and no recommendation of mercy, the disposition of the case should not be in doubt.
We find, if we look at the record of cases since 1961, the first year of the change, to ascertain whether or not any recommendations were made, that from the statistics reported on pages 100 to 103 of the White Paper on Capital Punishment, as brought up to date by some statistics that have been very kindly furnished to me by the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell), show there have been 30 capital cases since September, 1961. There have been 30 cases in which an individual has been convicted of capital murder.
In so far as recommendations are concerned, we find that in 12 of these cases the jury made no recommendation and in the other 18 cases the jury recommended mercy.

It is interesting to find too, Mr. Speaker, that out of those 30 cases the judge, who of course always has the right to make a recommendation, made no recommendation in 19 cases. The judge made a recommendation in 11. Further, it is interesting to note that the judge recommended mercy in two cases in which the jury did not recommend mercy. This, then, is the record with regard to recommendations. As I have said, out of 30 cases the jury recommended mercy in 18 and made no recommendation in 12.
I refer now to commutations. We find that since 1961, when the former government of which I was a member was in office, there were ten cases of persons convicted of capital murder which came before us. In eight of those cases the sentence was commuted to life imprisonment and in two cases the sentence was carried out. If we examine the question of recommendations we find that of the eight commutations, five were in cases where the jury recommended mercy. Of the three where there was no jury recommendation, two had been recommended to mercy by the judge.
There was a commutation, between September, 1961 and April, 1963, in only one case in which there was no recommendation whatever. If you examine the record since April, 1963, you will find there have been 20 convictions for capital murder which came before the cabinet and all 20 have been commuted. Of those, 13 had been recommended to mercy by the jury and 7 had no recommendation by either the judge or the jury. It is not my purpose, Mr. Speaker, to make any political condemnation here. However, speaking statistically, I would say that since April, 1963, there have been seven, what I would call doubtful cases where the government did not act in accordance with what I had believed would be accepted as the intent of the new law, namely, that where there was no recommendation in a conviction of capital murder there would be a certain execution. I mention this because I do believe this feature is a major reason for the unrest and concern which is felt about this whole matter in the country at the present time.
The other statistics which may or may not prove anything but certainly are a cause for concern, the kind of concern which I said would be felt if we have to vote on this motion, are statistics which have come before me from my own constituency. I feel they are typical of a mixed urban and rural constituency. The daily paper in Kamloops ran what
March 28, 1966

might be called a poll for three days. They inserted a small coupon in which the readers were asked to indicate broadly whether they favoured retention or abolition.
